No new combination here.

Field note. The notebook records where, when and how the observation was made. In this teaching case, two pots seem to dry at different rates; a memory of 'the drier one' would lose important context.
Pattern. Comparing the notes suggests that the sunnier pot dries sooner. A pattern gives us a question, not yet an explanation: the pots might also differ in size.
Hypothesis. One candidate explanation is that greater light exposure increases drying in this setup. It remains a hypothesis rather than a discovery about every plant or climate.
Testable question. If the proposed explanation matters, otherwise similar pots under different light should lose different amounts of water. That prediction makes a possible failure visible.
Calibrated scale. A known reference exposes an offset in the scale. Calibration ties readings to a standard; it does not remove every source of error.
Measurement series. Repeated readings reveal small fluctuations that a single reading would hide. Keep the variation rather than choosing the most pleasing number.

Controlled comparison. The teaching comparison changes light while holding pot size and starting water fixed. Controlling these conditions narrows the explanations; it does not guarantee all confounders vanished.
No new combination here.
Experimental protocol. The written protocol says what will be compared, measured and recorded. It turns a private trick into a procedure another person can attempt.
No new combination here.
Measurement record. The record pairs each reading with its conditions. Another observer can now ask whether the difference is larger than the measurement uncertainty.
Repeatable experiment. The arrangement can be repeated from the record. A later attempt may disagree: repeatability is an opportunity to test the result, not a promise of agreement.
We collect the tools this collection needs from the places we have already visited. Everything else stays where we left it. We collect the things needed for this scene along the way.

Counterexample. One low-income household and one wealthy household can pay the same amount while bearing very different burdens. That counterexample defeats the universal equal-burden claim, not every possible argument for the levy.

Argument. The speaker claims the new levy is fair because everyone pays the same amount. A reason is now visible, so an audience can challenge its relevance instead of merely disliking the conclusion.
Explicit premises. The hidden premise is that equal amounts imply equal burdens. Naming it reveals where people who agree about the figures may still disagree.

Valid argument. In this supplied example, 'all citizens covered by rule R must pay; this person is covered by R; therefore this person must pay' has a valid form. Validity does not establish that the rule or premises are just or true.
Ambiguity. The speakers have used 'equal' to mean both equal amounts and equal sacrifice. A shared word was concealing two different questions.
Disambiguated term. Here 'equal amount' refers only to the numerical payment. The clarified term prevents one meaning being silently substituted for another.
We collect the tools this collection needs from the places we have already visited. Everything else stays where we left it. We collect the things needed for this scene along the way.
Collation. The copies preserve different words in the same passage. Collation puts the alternatives beside one another without deciding that the oldest-looking copy must be right.
Variant table. A quoted opening phrase—the lemma—identifies the passage being discussed. This reconstruction does not give ancient Alexandrian commentary modern line numbers.
Textual family. Shared copying errors suggest relationships between these copies. This is the modern curator's tentative family reconstruction; borrowing between copies can defeat a simple tree.
No new combination here.
Reconstructed reading. The missing reading is proposed from the surviving variants and copying patterns. It remains a reconstruction, not recovered certainty, and is visibly marked as such.
Critical text. The editor distinguishes readable text from conjecture. A small uncertainty mark prevents the restoration from masquerading as an untouched ancient witness.
Critical edition. The text is accompanied by alternatives and explanations. Readers can inspect the editorial judgment rather than being asked to trust a silently repaired passage.
Draft translation. The first translation chooses one meaning for an ambiguous word. Its fluency is useful, but does not prove it preserved every implication of the source.
Annotated translation. A note explains the rejected meaning and why the context favored this one. The translation now exposes an interpretive decision instead of hiding it.
No new combination here.
Parallel edition. Source text and translation can be compared passage by passage. The parallel edition gives readers a way to disagree with the translator.

playerReport: Voluntary end of sitting after completing stage 3, not the campaign ending and not a technical block. 33 attempts, 27 accepted, 25 creations, 2 advances. Opening pots gave scientific-method labels a concrete anchor; calibration limits, retaining variation and repeatability allowing disagreement were worthwhile. Early plausible combinations failed with no explanation; empty hints felt like dead-end declarations although later-created partners worked. Stage 2 was smoother and I explored ambiguity/context beyond the goals because equal payments versus equal sacrifice mattered. The valid-argument output switched from levy fairness premises to a different rule-R example, weakening continuity. Stage 3 taught the useful caveat that copying between manuscripts can defeat a simple family tree, but supplied no actual variant words or foreign word to judge. I increasingly felt I was assembling labels for intellectual work rather than doing that work. Ending this sitting because the term-plus-modifier chains have become routine. Mild curiosity about later topics remains, but no strong immediate desire to return. Logical interface only; no graphics or touch assessment.
